one_liner: 2017 C++-to-WebAssembly image/video filter set (Sobel, 3x3 convolutions, colour tweaks) with a pure-JS fallback; faster only on the heavy filters.
what_it_does: A drop-in browser script (lib/webdsp.js plus Emscripten glue and a prebuilt webdsp_c.wasm) that exposes over 30 filters on canvas RGBA data: grayScale, brighten, invert, noise, a Sobel edge filter, a generic 3x3 convFilter (blur, sharpen and other presets) and a family of 'multiFilter' colour effects. loadWASM() returns a promise for an object of plain JS functions that take a Uint8ClampedArray (plus width/height) and return the filtered pixels, which the caller copies back with pixels.data.set(). When WebAssembly is missing it loads lib/webdsp_polyfill.js and returns the same function names implemented in JavaScript.
how_it_is_fast: There is no special algorithm: the C++ loops (scalar Sobel with a separate grayscale buffer, direct non-separable 3x3 convolution in float, per-byte colour arithmetic) are compiled with emcc -O3 through asm2wasm, so the gain comes only from running typed integer/float loops in WebAssembly instead of the JIT-compiled JS of the same loops. Each call mallocs a buffer in the WASM heap, copies the frame in (as bytes, or as Float32 for convFilter and noise, which quadruples the copy), runs the loop and hands back a view; that copy overhead is why simple per-pixel filters do not win.
when_to_use: Learning or teaching how a 2017-style Emscripten module is wrapped for canvas pixel processing; the C++ file is under 150 lines.
Prototyping edge detection (sobelFilter) or repeated 3x3 convolutions (blur with count=3) on small video frames, the only filters users reported as clearly faster than the JS path.
Vendoring a single filter loop into your own, modern WASM build after reviewing it, since the code is MIT-licensed and tiny.
when_not_to_use: Simple per-pixel filters (grayscale, invert, brighten, colour presets): users in issue #25 measured the WASM path 10-99% slower than the JS fallback in Chrome 61-63 and Firefox because of the copy in and out of the WASM heap.
Frames above about 1.3 megapixels with sobelFilter: it puts an int[width*height] variable-length array on a 5 MB stack (see gotchas), so 1080p input runs past the stack into the heap.

Anything production-facing: abandoned since 2017-06-05, the shipped .wasm does not match the source, there is no worker or OffscreenCanvas support, and the demo link in the README (tiny.cc/webdsp) now redirects to an affiliate spam page (issue #29).

Pipelines that need exact or portable results: brighten does not saturate, grayScale only copies the red channel, multiFilter wraps in C++ but clamps in JS, and convFilter ignores its bias argument in the WASM path.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (Emscripten glue and prebuilt .wasm are in lib/); rebuilding needs an emsdk checkout at ../emsdk with the 2017 asm2wasm toolchain
integration.min_toolchain: Browser with WebAssembly (binary version 1) and fetch, served over HTTP; rebuild script targets 2017 Emscripten (BINARYEN_IMPRECISE, asm2wasm) and BSD sed (macOS)
integration.platforms: Desktop browsers; the demo page states WebAssembly was not yet supported on mobile at the time
integration.thread_safety: not documented; one global Emscripten Module and heap on the main thread, wrappers use the global _malloc/HEAPU8
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the WASM object and jsFallback() expose the same function names, but outputs differ for the multiFilter family (wrap vs clamp), convFilter (bias ignored, clamping), Sobel borders and the eight filters listed in the README TODO

gotchas: Shipped binary does not match the source: lib/webdsp_c.wasm was last rebuilt 2017-03-29, before the 2017-04-02 brighten fix (commit 691a996), and exports _multiFilterFloat, which cpp/webdsp.cpp and compileWASM.sh no longer contain; rebuilding from source breaks the eight wrappers that call it (forest, romance, hippo, longhorn, moss, tingle, swamp, robbery), and the shipped brighten likely still has the doubled overflow check.

sobelFilter declares int grayData[width*height] on the stack; the shipped glue sets TOTAL_STACK to 5,242,880 bytes with an upward-growing fastcomp stack directly below the malloc heap and the binary imports no stack-overflow abort, so frames over about 1.31 M pixels (1920x1080 needs 8.3 MB) silently overwrite the heap that holds the input frame.

Every wrapper calls _free(mem) and then returns HEAPU8/HEAPF32.subarray(mem, ...), a view of freed memory; it is only safe if the caller copies it before any other allocation, and multiFilter reads data[i + width*4] past the end of the buffer on the last row.

The global 'var Module = {}', fixed './lib/' fetch paths and a sed patch of the glue's 'else{doRun()}' string mean it clashes with any other Emscripten module on the page and cannot be rebuilt with a current Emscripten without rework.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when you want a small, readable example of canvas filtering in WASM; for measured wins on pixel work BlazeDiff core-wasm (about 10x over pixelmatch at 4K) or the TensorFlow.js WASM backend are maintained and benchmarked, and iswasmfast is the better reference for when WASM actually beats JS.
verified_claims_summary: The repository has no benchmark; the README only says convolution and edge filters 'will run very slowly or hang the browser' without WebAssembly. The companion web-dsp-demo page times one video frame per path with performance.now() (WASM time includes malloc and both copies, the JS path filters in place, and both are given canvas.clientWidth as the image width), and independent users in issue #25 (2017-2018, Chrome 61-63, Firefox Nightly on an i7-6600U, a Pixel phone, a 2014 MacBook Air) found WASM 10-99% slower on most filters but 10-20x faster on Super Edge (Sobel) and 50-100% faster on Gaussian Blur; no maintainer replied.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-06-05 (open PR #23 and issues #24-#29 unanswered); MIT LICENSE file versus ISC in package.json, small enough to read in minutes, but treat it as a historical example rather than a library, and do not follow the README demo link.
